questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Deep transverse fissure on the visceral surface of the liver, bounded anteriorly by the quadrate lobe and posteriorly by the caudate lobe, transmitting the portal triad structures.
questions.keyConcept: The porta hepatis serves as the hilum of the liver, transmitting the hepatic portal vein (posteriorly), hepatic artery proper (anterior-left), and bile ducts (anterior-right), enveloped in Glisson's capsule.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Centrally located transverse hepatic hilum fissure between the caudate process/lobe above and quadrate lobe below, conveying the portal vein, hepatic artery branches, and hepatic bile ducts.
questions.keyConcept: The porta hepatis forms the horizontal crossbar of the 'H-shaped' visceral surface of the liver and transmits the components of the portal triad within the free margin of the lesser omentum.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Anterior-inferior longitudinal groove situated on the visceral surface between the left anatomical lobe and the quadrate lobe, housing the obliterated umbilical vein.
questions.keyConcept: The fissure for ligamentum teres forms the anterior part of the left longitudinal limb of the hepatic 'H' groove, extending from the inferior border of the liver to the left end of the porta hepatis.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Distinct, rectangular lobe situated on the posterosuperior visceral surface between the fissure for ligamentum venosum (left) and groove for IVC (right), superior to the porta hepatis.
questions.keyConcept: The caudate lobe (Spigelian lobe / Couinaud segment I) receives vascular branches from both right and left portal triads and drains directly into the IVC via small independent hepatic veins.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Four-sided (rectangular) lobe on the inferior visceral surface, bounded by the fossa for gallbladder on the right, fissure for ligamentum teres on the left, and porta hepatis posteriorly.
questions.keyConcept: Though anatomically part of the right lobe of the liver, the quadrate lobe functionally belongs to the left liver (Couinaud segment IV) because it receives blood supply from the left hepatic artery and left branch of the portal vein.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Vertical sulcus situated on the posterior surface between the caudate lobe and bare area of the right lobe, accommodating the inferior vena cava.
questions.keyConcept: The groove for the IVC forms the posterior part of the right longitudinal limb of the visceral 'H'; hepatic veins emerge here directly to empty into the inferior vena cava.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Large non-peritoneal triangular area on the posterior/diaphragmatic surface of the right lobe of the liver, bounded by the superior and inferior layers of the coronary ligament.
questions.keyConcept: The bare area of the liver is in direct contact with the diaphragm without intervening peritoneum; its lymphatic vessels drain directly through the diaphragm into posterior mediastinal lymph nodes.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Narrow, deep vertical cleft on the postero-inferior surface separating the caudate lobe from the left anatomical lobe, containing the fibrous remnant of the ductus venosus.
questions.keyConcept: The fissure for ligamentum venosum forms the posterior part of the left longitudinal limb of the hepatic 'H' and provides attachment for the two layers of the lesser omentum.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Large blue venous vessel occupying the deep vertical groove on the posterior surface of the liver to the right of the caudate lobe.
questions.keyConcept: The inferior vena cava (IVC) receives the major hepatic veins directly before piercing the central tendon of the diaphragm at the level of the T8 vertebra.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Four-sided, rectangular lobe on the visceral surface situated between the gallbladder fossa laterally and fissure for ligamentum teres medially, anterior to the porta hepatis.
questions.keyConcept: The quadrate lobe is related infero-posteriorly to the pylorus of the stomach and the first part of the duodenum; functionally, it constitutes Couinaud segment IV.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Prominent lobe on the posterior surface of the liver, situated between the groove for the IVC on the right, fissure for ligamentum venosum on the left, and porta hepatis inferiorly.
questions.keyConcept: The caudate lobe features two small processes: the papillary process extending to the left, and the caudate process connecting it to the right lobe between the IVC and porta hepatis (forming the superior boundary of the epiploic foramen of Winslow).

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Fibrous round cord running in the free inferior edge of the falciform ligament and along the fissure for ligamentum teres on the visceral surface.
questions.keyConcept: The ligamentum teres hepatis is the obliterated remnant of the left umbilical vein, which carried oxygenated and nutrient-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Slender fibrous cord lying within the deep vertical fissure between the caudate lobe and the anatomical left lobe, extending toward the IVC.
questions.keyConcept: The ligamentum venosum is the fibrous remnant of the fetal ductus venosus, which shunted oxygenated umbilical vein blood directly to the IVC, bypassing the hepatic sinusoids.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Greenish pyriform reservoir attached to the visceral surface of the anatomical right lobe of the liver, comprising a fundus, body, infundibulum, and neck.
questions.keyConcept: The gallbladder concentrates and stores hepatic bile; its neck narrows into the cystic duct, which contains the spiral fold (spiral valve of Heister) and joins the common hepatic duct to form the bile duct.

questions.text: This picture represents which surface of liver
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Smooth, convex, dome-shaped surface of the liver conforming to the concavity of the diaphragm, divided into anterior, superior, and posterior parts and split by the falciform ligament.
questions.keyConcept: The diaphragmatic surface of the liver is separated from the visceral surface anteriorly by the sharp inferior border; it is covered by visceral peritoneum except at the bare area posteriorly.

questions.text: This picture represents which surface of liver
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Postero-inferior surface of the liver displaying visceral organ impressions, the H-shaped fissures, porta hepatis, gallbladder fossa, and caudate and quadrate lobes.
questions.keyConcept: The visceral surface is directed postero-inferiorly and to the left, bearing impressions from abdominal organs including the stomach, duodenum, right kidney, right suprarenal gland, and right colic flexure.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The falciform ligament is a double-layered sickle-shaped peritoneal fold attaching the diaphragmatic surface of the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm. Morphologically and anatomically, its attachment divides the liver into two unequal lobes: a large anatomical right lobe (approx. 5/6 of liver mass) and a smaller anatomical left lobe (approx. 1/6).
questions.keyConcept: Anatomical vs. functional liver lobes: The falciform ligament anatomically divides the liver into unequal right and left lobes, whereas Cantlie's line physiologically divides it into two roughly equal functional halves.

questions.text: This imaginary line divides liver into
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The highlighted plane represents Cantlie's line (principal plane of the liver), which courses obliquely from the gallbladder fossa on the visceral surface to the left border of the inferior vena cava. This plane divides the liver into right and left functional (physiological) lobes of approximately equal parenchymal volume.
questions.keyConcept: Functional lobes of liver: Demarcated by Cantlie's line from the IVC groove to the gallbladder fossa; splits the liver into two functionally equal halves based on independent hepatic arterial, portal venous, and biliary distributions.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Large triangular non-peritoneal area located on the posterior surface of the right anatomical lobe of the liver. It is delimited superiorly by the superior layer of the coronary ligament, inferiorly by the inferior layer of the coronary ligament, laterally by the right triangular ligament, and medially by the groove for the inferior vena cava.
questions.keyConcept: Bare area of the liver: Direct non-peritoneal contact zone between the liver and diaphragm; forms important retroperitoneal portosystemic venous communications and is enclosed by the coronary ligaments.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Distinct rounded or nipple-like projection (processus papillaris) extending from the inferior and left aspect of the caudate lobe of the liver. It projects downward and medially into the superior recess of the omental bursa (lesser sac), just behind the porta hepatis and to the right of the fissure for ligamentum venosum.
questions.keyConcept: Papillary process of caudate lobe: Small rounded nodule projecting from the lower left border of the caudate lobe into the omental bursa, adjacent to the porta hepatis.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Narrow transverse ridge of hepatic parenchyma connecting the lower right corner of the caudate lobe to the visceral surface of the anatomical right lobe. It courses between the porta hepatis anteriorly and the groove for the inferior vena cava posteriorly, directly forming the superior margin (roof) of the epiploic foramen of Winslow.
questions.keyConcept: Caudate process: Narrow parenchymal bridge linking the caudate lobe to the right lobe between the IVC and porta hepatis; serves as the roof of the epiploic foramen.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Triangular depressed area situated on the bare area of the posterior aspect of the right lobe of the liver, positioned immediately adjacent to the right margin of the inferior vena cava and superior to the renal impression. It directly accommodates the right suprarenal gland without peritoneal intervention.
questions.keyConcept: Right suprarenal impression: Located on the bare area of the liver directly to the right of the IVC groove; lacks peritoneal lining and rests in direct apposition with the right suprarenal gland.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Broad, deep, smooth concave impression occupying the upper and posterior portion of the visceral surface of the right hepatic lobe. It is situated directly below the inferior layer of the coronary ligament and lateral to the duodenal impression, accommodating the upper half of the anterior surface of the right kidney.
questions.keyConcept: Renal impression of liver: The largest impression on the visceral surface of the right hepatic lobe, related to the right kidney and forming the anterior boundary of the hepatorenal recess (Morison's pouch).

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Shallow impression on the visceral surface of the right lobe of the liver located immediately adjacent to the neck of the gallbladder and gallbladder fossa, medial to the renal impression and inferior to the caudate process. It directly contacts the descending (second) part of the duodenum.
questions.keyConcept: Duodenal impression on liver: Located on the right lobe between the gallbladder fossa and renal impression, in direct contact with the descending (2nd) part of the duodenum.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Extensive, smooth, deep concavity occupying almost the entire visceral (inferior) surface of the anatomical left lobe of the liver. It lies anterior and to the left of the fissure for ligamentum venosum and is molded over the anterior wall of the body and fundus of the stomach.
questions.keyConcept: Gastric impression of liver: Covers the vast majority of the visceral surface of the left hepatic lobe, molded over the anterior aspect of the stomach body and fundus.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Shallow groove situated on the posterosuperior aspect of the visceral surface of the left lobe of the liver, adjacent to the upper extremity of the fissure for the ligamentum venosum. It is produced by direct contact with the anterior surface of the abdominal segment of the esophagus.
questions.keyConcept: Esophageal impression: Notch-like groove on the visceral surface of the left lobe of the liver near the upper end of the fissure for ligamentum venosum, related to the abdominal esophagus.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Flat, shallow impression situated at the anterior and inferior margin of the visceral surface of the right lobe of the liver, immediately behind the sharp inferior border and lateral to the gallbladder fossa. It directly accommodates the right colic (hepatic) flexure.
questions.keyConcept: Colic impression of liver: Occupies the anteroinferior territory of the right lobe's visceral surface, contacting the hepatic flexure where the ascending colon transitions into the transverse colon.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Extrahepatic biliary duct (labeled 1) formed within the porta hepatis by the confluence of the right and left hepatic ducts. It descends in the right free border of the lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal ligament) anterior to the portal vein until joined on its right lateral side by the cystic duct.
questions.keyConcept: Common hepatic duct: Formed by the union of right and left hepatic ducts, descends in the hepatoduodenal ligament, and joins the cystic duct to form the bile duct (common bile duct).

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: S-shaped extrahepatic biliary duct (labeled 2) measuring 3–4 cm in length, emerging from the neck of the gallbladder. It passes posteroinferiorly within the lesser omentum, containing mucosal spiral folds (valve of Heister), and joins the common hepatic duct at an acute angle.
questions.keyConcept: Cystic duct: Transports bile to and from the gallbladder; contains the spiral valve of Heister preventing duct collapse; forms the inferior boundary of the hepatobiliary triangle of Calot.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Main extrahepatic biliary channel (labeled 3) formed by the junction of the cystic duct and common hepatic duct. It descends within the free margin of the lesser omentum (supraduodenal part), passes behind the first part of the duodenum (retroduodenal part), and grooves the posterior head of the pancreas before entering the descending duodenum.
questions.keyConcept: Bile duct (ductus choledochus): Formed by the convergence of the common hepatic and cystic ducts; courses through supraduodenal, retroduodenal, and infraduodenal segments to terminate at the ampulla of Vater.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Dilated terminal hepatopancreatic confluence (labeled 4) formed by the union of the bile duct and the main pancreatic duct (of Wirsung). It pierces the posteromedial wall of the second (descending) part of the duodenum, surrounded by the sphincter of Oddi, and opens into the duodenal lumen at the major duodenal papilla.
questions.keyConcept: Hepatopancreatic ampulla (Ampulla of Vater): Shared terminal dilatation of the bile duct and main pancreatic duct entering the 2nd part of the duodenum; impaction of gallstones at this site can precipitate acute biliary pancreatitis.

questions.text: Which surface marked with the arrow
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Broad, completely smooth, and convex surface of the spleen facing posterolaterally and superiorly. It is devoid of a hilum or visceral impressions and is molded against the abdominal surface of the diaphragm, which separates it from the left pleural cavity and ribs 9–11.
questions.keyConcept: Diaphragmatic surface of spleen: Smooth and convex, related via the diaphragm to the left costodiaphragmatic recess and shafts of the 9th, 10th, and 11th ribs.

questions.text: Which surface represented with this picture
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Irregular medial-facing surface of the spleen characterized by the long central splenic hilum transmitting the splenic vessels, and partitioned by distinct ridges into gastric, renal, colic, and pancreatic contact impressions.
questions.keyConcept: Visceral surface of spleen: Irregular and concave, contains the hilum transmitting the splenic artery and vein, and bears impressions for the stomach, left kidney, left colic flexure, and tail of the pancreas.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Broad, expanded, flattened extremity of the spleen (extremitas anterior), directed anteroinferiorly and laterally. It is reliably recognized by its direct proximity to the splenic notch(es) on the sharp superior border, and on the visceral aspect it supports the colic impression resting upon the phrenicocolic ligament.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior (lateral) end of spleen: Expanded and border-like, directed downward and forward toward the left colic flexure; distinguished by its proximity to the notches on the superior border.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Blunt, rounded, tapered pole of the spleen (extremitas posterior), directed posterosuperiorly and medially toward the vertebral column. It is smooth and rounded, situated well away from the splenic notches, and rests against the upper pole of the left kidney and left suprarenal gland.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior (medial) end of spleen: Rounded and blunt, directed medially and upward toward the vertebral column (level of T10), resting on the upper pole of the left kidney.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Large, smooth, concave impression (labeled 1) occupying the visceral surface of the spleen superior and anterior to the splenic hilum, bounded superiorly by the notched superior border. It accommodates the posterior wall of the gastric fundus and body.
questions.keyConcept: Gastric impression of spleen: Located above and anterior to the hilum, this is the largest visceral impression on the spleen and is directly related to the posterior wall of the stomach.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Concave impression located on the visceral surface of the spleen inferior and posterior to the splenic hilum, separated from the gastric impression by the intermediate border. It accommodates the anterior surface of the upper pole of the left kidney and left suprarenal gland.
questions.keyConcept: Splenic visceral impressions: The renal impression lies below and behind the hilum (related to the left kidney), whereas the gastric impression lies above and anterior to the hilum.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Flat, triangular impression situated at the anterior (expanded) end/lateral extremity of the visceral surface of the spleen, bounded by the anterior pole, inferior border, and the splenic hilum. It rests directly upon the left colic (splenic) flexure and the phrenicocolic ligament.
questions.keyConcept: Colic impression of spleen: Located at the anterior pole/angle, resting on the left colic flexure and supported by the phrenicocolic ligament (sustentaculum lienis).

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Small, smooth facet located on the visceral surface of the spleen between the lower part of the splenic hilum and the colic impression. It makes direct contact with the tail of the pancreas within the lienorenal (splenorenal) ligament.
questions.keyConcept: Pancreatic impression of spleen: Positioned between the lower end of the hilum and the colic impression, accommodating the tail of the pancreas which enters the splenorenal ligament.

questions.text: Identify the skeletal relationship of the diaphragmatic surface of the spleen:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The smooth, convex diaphragmatic surface of the spleen faces posterolaterally and superiorly, molded to the abdominal surface of the diaphragm. It is related through the diaphragm and left costodiaphragmatic recess of the pleura to the shafts of the 9th, 10th, and 11th left ribs, with its long axis oriented parallel to the 10th rib.
questions.keyConcept: Surface anatomy of spleen: Lies in the left hypochondrium underlying the 9th, 10th, and 11th ribs, separated from them by the diaphragm and costodiaphragmatic pleural recess; rib fractures here pose high risk of splenic rupture.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Paired major vascular channels (artery and vein) emerging from beneath the lower border of the neck of the pancreas and crossing anterior to the uncinate process of the pancreas and the third (horizontal) part of the duodenum before descending into the root of the mesentery.
questions.keyConcept: Superior mesenteric vessels (SMA & SMV): Emerge below the pancreatic neck, cross anterior to the uncinate process and 3rd part of the duodenum; compression can cause superior mesenteric artery (Wilkie's) syndrome.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Main arterial trunk arising from the anterior aspect of the abdominal aorta at L1 (approx. 1 cm below the celiac trunk). It passes posterior to the neck of the pancreas, anterior to the uncinate process and 3rd part of the duodenum, and enters the root of the mesentery, coursing downward and to the right toward the right iliac fossa.
questions.keyConcept: Superior mesenteric artery (SMA): Originates at L1, passes over the uncinate process and 3rd part of duodenum, supplies midgut derivatives from major duodenal papilla to proximal two-thirds of transverse colon.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Main trunk of the superior mesenteric artery (labeled D) coursing obliquely downward and to the right in the mesentery root, giving off colic branches from its right/concave side and multiple intestinal (jejunal and ileal) branches from its left/convex side.
questions.keyConcept: SMA arborization: The main trunk gives colic branches (middle colic, right colic, ileocolic) from its right side and intestinal branches (jejunal and ileal) from its left side.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Arises from the anterior/right aspect of the SMA just below the neck of the pancreas (labeled A). It enters the transverse mesocolon, coursing upward and forward, and divides into right and left branches to supply the transverse colon and anastomose with the right colic and left colic arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Middle colic artery: First colic branch of the SMA, travels within the transverse mesocolon to supply the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon, forming an anastomosis contributing to the marginal artery of Drummond.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Arises from the right side of the SMA (labeled B) or via a common trunk with the ileocolic artery. It courses retroperitoneally to the right across the posterior abdominal wall, passing in front of the testicular/ovarian vessels, right ureter, and psoas major to reach and supply the ascending colon.
questions.keyConcept: Right colic artery: Arises from the right side of the SMA, courses retroperitoneally to supply the ascending colon, dividing into ascending (anastomosing with middle colic) and descending (anastomosing with ileocolic) branches.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Lowest branch arising from the right concave side of the SMA (labeled C). It courses downward and laterally toward the right iliac fossa across the right ureter and psoas major, terminating near the ileocecal junction into superior (colic) and inferior branches (ileal, anterior and posterior cecal, and appendicular artery).
questions.keyConcept: Ileocolic artery: Lowest right branch of the SMA, supplies the terminal ileum, cecum, appendix (via appendicular artery), and proximal ascending colon.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Distal intestinal branches (labeled B) arising from the left convex side of the SMA supplying the ileum. They are anatomically characterized by forming multiple tiered vascular arcades (3 to 5 cascades) with very short, numerous straight terminal vessels (vasa recta) and abundant mesenteric fat extending up to the intestinal wall.
questions.keyConcept: Ileal arterial arcade architecture: Characterized by complex multi-tiered arterial arcades (3-5 cascades) and short, closely spaced vasa recta, distinguished from jejunal branches.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Proximal intestinal branches (labeled C) arising from the upper part of the left convex border of the SMA heading toward the jejunum in the upper left quadrant. They are anatomically characterized by 1 or 2 simple arterial arcades giving rise to long, tall, straight terminal vessels (vasa recta) with minimal mesenteric fat creating translucent peritoneal 'windows'.
questions.keyConcept: Jejunal arterial arcade architecture: Features 1-2 simple arcades with long, widely spaced straight arteries (vasa recta) and clear mesenteric windows, contrasted with the multiple arcades and short vasa recta of the ileum.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Short, wide arterial stump (approx. 1.25 cm long) originating directly from the anterior aspect of the abdominal aorta immediately below the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm at the level of the T12/L1 vertebral junction. It rapidly trifurcates into the left gastric, splenic, and common hepatic arteries to supply the embryological foregut.
questions.keyConcept: Celiac trunk: Originates from the abdominal aorta at T12, supplies foregut derivatives via its 3 classic branches: left gastric artery, splenic artery, and common hepatic artery.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Smallest branch of the celiac trunk that ascends obliquely upward and to the left toward the abdominal esophagus and cardiac orifice of the stomach within the gastropancreatic fold. It gives esophageal branches and arches downward along the lesser curvature of the stomach within the lesser omentum to anastomose with the right gastric artery.
questions.keyConcept: Left gastric artery: Smallest celiac branch, runs in the lesser omentum along the lesser curvature, supplying the lower esophagus and cardiac/body region of the stomach.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Largest and most tortuous branch of the celiac trunk. It courses horizontally to the left along the superior border of the body and tail of the pancreas, in the floor of the lesser sac (stomach bed), and passes within the splenorenal ligament to enter the splenic hilum, giving pancreatic branches, short gastric arteries, and the left gastroepiploic artery.
questions.keyConcept: Splenic artery: Highly tortuous branch coursing along the upper border of the pancreas in the splenorenal ligament; gives short gastric arteries (fundus) and left gastroepiploic artery.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Arises from the hepatic artery proper (or common hepatic) near the pylorus. It descends to the pyloric end of the stomach and courses from right to left along the lesser curvature within the lesser omentum, supplying both surfaces of the antrum and lesser curvature and anastomosing with the left gastric artery.
questions.keyConcept: Right gastric artery: Arises from the hepatic proper artery (or common hepatic), courses along the lesser curvature to anastomose with the left gastric artery.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Arises from the splenic artery near the splenic hilum, traverses the gastrosplenic ligament to reach the greater curvature of the stomach, and runs from left to right between the anterior two layers of the greater omentum, supplying the gastric wall and omentum and anastomosing with the right gastroepiploic artery.
questions.keyConcept: Left gastroepiploic (gastro-omental) artery: Originates from the splenic artery within the gastrosplenic ligament and courses along the greater curvature to anastomose with the right gastroepiploic artery.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Arises as a terminal branch of the gastroduodenal artery behind the first part of the duodenum. It passes along the greater curvature of the stomach from right to left between the anterior layers of the greater omentum, giving branches to the stomach walls and greater omentum before anastomosing with the left gastroepiploic artery.
questions.keyConcept: Right gastroepiploic (gastro-omental) artery: Terminal branch of the gastroduodenal artery running along the greater curvature, forming an omental arc with the left gastroepiploic artery.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Continuation of the common hepatic artery beyond the origin of the gastroduodenal artery. It ascends within the free margin of the lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal ligament) anterior to the portal vein and to the left of the common bile duct, terminating near the porta hepatis by dividing into right and left hepatic arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Proper hepatic artery: Ascends in the free edge of the lesser omentum (portal triad: artery left, bile duct right, portal vein posterior) to supply the liver and gallbladder.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Intermediate-sized branch of the celiac trunk running forward and to the right retroperitoneally along the superior border of the head of the pancreas and across the crus of the diaphragm and IVC. At the upper border of the first part of the duodenum, it terminates by dividing into the gastroduodenal artery and the hepatic artery proper.
questions.keyConcept: Common hepatic artery: Courses rightward along the upper border of the pancreatic head to bifurcate into gastroduodenal and proper hepatic arteries.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Arises from the hepatic artery (proper or common) and descends to the pyloric end of the stomach, running from right to left along the lesser curvature within the lesser omentum to anastomose with the left gastric artery.
questions.keyConcept: The lesser curvature of the stomach is supplied by an arterial arcade formed by the right gastric artery (from hepatic artery proper/common) and left gastric artery (from celiac trunk) within the hepatogastric ligament.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Large horizontal vein formed at the splenic hilum, coursing to the right behind the body and tail of the pancreas and stomach, receiving the short gastric, left gastroepiploic, and inferior mesenteric veins before uniting with the SMV.
questions.keyConcept: The splenic vein runs in the retroperitoneal groove behind the pancreas and joins the superior mesenteric vein behind the neck of the pancreas to form the hepatic portal vein.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Runs along the lesser curvature of the stomach within the lesser omentum from left to right, receiving esophageal tributaries and draining directly into the portal vein.
questions.keyConcept: The left gastric (coronary) vein is a major tributary of the portal vein and forms a crucial portosystemic anastomosis with the esophageal branches of the azygos vein, dilating into esophageal varices in portal hypertension.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Ascends vertically in the retroperitoneum on the left side of the posterior abdominal wall, draining blood from the rectum, sigmoid colon, and descending colon, typically terminating in the splenic vein behind the pancreatic body.
questions.keyConcept: The inferior mesenteric vein (IMV) drains hindgut derivatives and typically empties into the splenic vein (or occasionally into the SMV or splenomesenteric junction).

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Large vertical vein ascending in the root of the mesentery to the right of the superior mesenteric artery, passing anterior to the 3rd (horizontal) part of the duodenum and uncinate process of the pancreas to join the splenic vein.
questions.keyConcept: The superior mesenteric vein (SMV) drains midgut structures (small intestine, cecum, ascending colon, and transverse colon) and unites with the splenic vein behind the neck of the pancreas to form the hepatic portal vein.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Formed behind the neck of the pancreas by the confluence of the splenic and superior mesenteric veins; ascends obliquely to the right within the hepatoduodenal ligament of the lesser omentum posterior to the proper hepatic artery and common bile duct.
questions.keyConcept: The hepatic portal vein is formed at the L1-L2 level behind the neck of the pancreas; within the free margin of the lesser omentum, it lies posterior to the proper hepatic artery (left) and common bile duct (right).

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Arises from the anterior aspect of the abdominal aorta approximately 3-4 cm above the aortic bifurcation at vertebral level L3, giving origin to the left colic artery, sigmoid arteries, and terminating as the superior rectal artery.
questions.keyConcept: The inferior mesenteric artery (IMA) is the artery of the hindgut; it originates at L3 behind the third part of the duodenum and supplies the distal third of the transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, and proximal rectum.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: First branch of the inferior mesenteric artery, coursing retroperitoneally upward and to the left across the psoas major and gonadal vessels before dividing into ascending and descending branches.
questions.keyConcept: The left colic artery is the primary branch of the IMA supplying the descending colon and splenic flexure, dividing into an ascending branch (which anastomoses with the middle colic artery) and a descending branch.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Branch of the left colic artery running vertically upward toward the splenic flexure and left portion of the transverse colon to anastomose with the middle colic artery, contributing to the marginal artery of Drummond.
questions.keyConcept: The ascending branch of the left colic artery provides blood supply to the splenic flexure and anastomoses with the left branch of the middle colic artery, completing the marginal artery (arc of Riolan / Drummond's marginal artery).

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Lower division of the left colic artery running downward toward the descending colon to anastomose with the highest sigmoid artery along the mesenteric border.
questions.keyConcept: The descending branch of the left colic artery supplies the descending colon and anastomoses inferiorly with the superior sigmoid artery, sustaining the continuous marginal artery arcade along the hindgut.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Two to four branches arising from the inferior mesenteric artery that descend obliquely to the left across the psoas major and enter the sigmoid mesocolon to supply the sigmoid colon.
questions.keyConcept: The sigmoid arteries enter the sigmoid mesocolon to supply the pelvic/sigmoid colon, forming arterial arcades that anastomose with the left colic artery above and superior rectal artery below.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Direct continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery as it crosses the left common iliac vessels to descend into the pelvic cavity within the root of the sigmoid mesocolon/mesorectum.
questions.keyConcept: The superior rectal (superior hemorrhoidal) artery is the terminal continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery; it bifurcates around S3 to supply the upper rectum down to the pectinate line.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Pear-shaped sac lodged in the gallbladder fossa on the visceral surface of the right lobe of the liver, consisting of a fundus, body, infundibulum, and neck.
questions.keyConcept: The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile produced by the liver; its fundus projects beyond the inferior border of the liver at the tip of the right 9th costal cartilage (Murphy's point).

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Convoluted duct approximately 3-4 cm long connecting the neck of the gallbladder to the common hepatic duct, containing internal mucosal folds known as the spiral valves of Heister.
questions.keyConcept: The cystic duct connects the gallbladder to the common hepatic duct to form the common bile duct; it forms the inferior boundary of the cystohepatic triangle of Calot.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Duct exiting the right lobe of the liver at the porta hepatis on the anatomical right side of the biliary bifurcation, uniting with the left hepatic duct to form the common hepatic duct.
questions.keyConcept: The right hepatic duct drains bile from anatomical segments V, VI, VII, and VIII of the right functional liver and joins the left hepatic duct at the porta hepatis.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Duct emerging from the porta hepatis on the anatomical left side, draining the left functional liver (segments II, III, IV) and joining the right hepatic duct to form the common hepatic duct.
questions.keyConcept: The left hepatic duct drains segments II, III, and IV (and part of I); it has a longer extrahepatic course than the right hepatic duct before they merge to form the common hepatic duct.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Formed at the porta hepatis by the convergence of the right and left hepatic ducts; descends approximately 4 cm within the hepatoduodenal ligament before receiving the cystic duct.
questions.keyConcept: The common hepatic duct descends within the free edge of the lesser omentum to the right of the proper hepatic artery and anterior to the portal vein, joining the cystic duct to form the common bile duct.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Main extrahepatic biliary channel formed by the confluence of the common hepatic duct and cystic duct; descends behind the first part of the duodenum and head of the pancreas to enter the second part of the duodenum.
questions.keyConcept: The common bile duct passes through supraduodenal, retroduodenal, infraduodenal, and intraduodenal portions, entering the second part of the duodenum at the major duodenal papilla via the ampulla of Vater.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Extends horizontally through the pancreas from tail to head, joining the terminal part of the common bile duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater) in the wall of the descending duodenum.
questions.keyConcept: The main pancreatic duct (duct of Wirsung) joins the common bile duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla of Vater, which is guarded by the sphincter of Oddi and opens at the major duodenal papilla in the medial wall of the second part of the duodenum.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The quadrate lobe of the liver is related on its visceral surface from superior to inferior to: the lesser omentum (L, most superior), pylorus and first part of the duodenum (P, middle), and transverse colon (T, most inferior), forming the classic mnemonic 'L-P-T'.
questions.keyConcept: The quadrate lobe of the liver lies on the visceral surface bounded by the gallbladder fossa on the right, fissure for ligamentum teres on the left, and porta hepatis superiorly; its visceral relations from superior to inferior follow the mnemonic 'L-P-T' (Lesser omentum, Pylorus/1st part duodenum, Transverse colon).

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Transverse section through the abdomen at the T12–L1 vertebral level, characterized by the presence of the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow) bounded anteriorly by the free margin of the lesser omentum (portal triad) and posteriorly by the inferior vena cava (IVC), along with the stomach, spleen, liver, and upper poles of both kidneys with suprarenal glands.
questions.keyConcept: A cross section at the T12–L1 level is defined by the epiploic foramen (omental bursa entrance), with the IVC posteriorly, the portal triad anteriorly, and both kidneys/adrenals flanking the aorta.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Paired strap-like muscle located on either side of the midline linea alba on the anterior abdominal wall, enclosed within the rectus sheath.
questions.keyConcept: The rectus abdominis is the primary vertical muscle of the anterior abdominal wall, separated from its contralateral partner by the linea alba and enclosed within the rectus sheath.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Midline fibrous band running vertically down the anterior abdominal wall between the medial borders of the two rectus abdominis muscles, formed by the decussation of aponeuroses of the abdominal flat muscles.
questions.keyConcept: The linea alba is an avascular fibrous raphe in the anterior midline of the abdomen formed by the fusion of the anterior and posterior rectus sheaths.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Large parenchymal organ occupying the right hypochondrium and epigastrium, bounded peripherally by the diaphragm and body wall, and showing intrahepatic vascular channels.
questions.keyConcept: The liver is the largest solid abdominal organ, located primarily in the right hypochondrium and epigastrium, directly beneath the diaphragm.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Hollow sac-like structure with characteristic green biliary mucosal lining seated in the fossa for the gallbladder on the visceral surface of the liver.
questions.keyConcept: The gallbladder resides in the gallbladder fossa on the inferior/visceral surface of the liver, storing and concentrating bile delivered via the cystic duct.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Prominent hollow muscular digestive organ in the left upper quadrant/epigastrium with a large lumen, thick muscular walls, and folded mucosa, situated anterior to the lesser sac and pancreas.
questions.keyConcept: The stomach lies in the left hypochondrium, epigastrium, and umbilical regions, anterior to the omental bursa (lesser sac) and bed of the stomach.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Double layer of peritoneum extending from the liver (porta hepatis and fissure for ligamentum venosum) to the lesser curvature of the stomach and first part of the duodenum, forming the anterior wall of the lesser sac.
questions.keyConcept: The lesser omentum consists of the hepatogastric and hepatoduodenal ligaments, connecting the stomach's lesser curvature to the liver and enclosing the portal triad along its free margin.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Peritoneal space (omental bursa) located posterior to the stomach and lesser omentum and anterior to the pancreas, communicating with the greater sac via the epiploic foramen.
questions.keyConcept: The lesser sac (omental bursa) is a large peritoneal diverticulum situated behind the stomach and lesser omentum, allowing frictionless stomach distension.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Large vascular lumen situated in the free margin of the lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal ligament) posterior to the hepatic artery and bile duct, and immediately anterior to the epiploic foramen.
questions.keyConcept: In the free border of the lesser omentum, the portal triad consists of the portal vein posteriorly, the bile duct anterolaterally (on the right), and the hepatic artery proper anteromedially (on the left).

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Large retroperitoneal venous structure situated to the right of the vertebral body and aorta, directly forming the posterior boundary of the epiploic foramen.
questions.keyConcept: The inferior vena cava (IVC) ascends retroperitoneally on the right side of the vertebral column and aorta, forming the definitive posterior boundary of the epiploic foramen of Winslow.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Large thick-walled arterial vessel positioned directly anterior to the lower thoracic/upper lumbar vertebral body (T12), situated between the crura of the diaphragm and medial to the IVC.
questions.keyConcept: The abdominal aorta enters the abdomen through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm at the T12 vertebral level, lying immediately anterior to the vertebral bodies and to the left of the IVC.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Bony vertebral body located in the posterior midline supporting the abdominal aorta and IVC anteriorly, corresponding to the T12 level at the epiploic foramen.
questions.keyConcept: The T12 vertebra forms the posterior skeletal landmark at the level of the aortic hiatus and epiploic foramen, flanked by the crura of the diaphragm.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Musculotendinous band arising from the anterior and lateral aspects of the upper lumbar/lower thoracic vertebral bodies on the left side of the aorta, medial to the left suprarenal gland.
questions.keyConcept: The left crus of the diaphragm arises from the upper two lumbar vertebral bodies and their intervertebral discs, lying to the left of the abdominal aorta.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Prominent musculotendinous band arising from the upper lumbar vertebral bodies on the right side of the aorta, situated between the abdominal aorta and the IVC.
questions.keyConcept: The right crus of the diaphragm is larger and longer than the left, arising from the bodies of L1–L3 and forming the muscular fibers of the esophageal hiatus.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Retroperitoneal bean-shaped parenchymal organ showing renal cortex and pelvis on the left side of the abdominal cavity, situated medial to the spleen and lateral to the aorta/left crus.
questions.keyConcept: The left kidney lies slightly higher than the right kidney (T11/T12 to L2/L3) and is related anteriorly to the stomach, pancreas, spleen, jejunum, and colic flexure.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Retroperitoneal parenchymal organ displayed on the right side of the cross section, situated posterior to the liver and lateral to the inferior vena cava and right crus.
questions.keyConcept: The right kidney lies lower than the left kidney due to the bulk of the right lobe of the liver, and is related anteriorly to the liver, duodenum, and right colic flexure.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Solid lymphoid organ located posterolaterally in the left hypochondrium, related to ribs 9–11 and positioned lateral to the left kidney and posterior to the stomach.
questions.keyConcept: The spleen is a highly vascular lymphatic organ situated beneath the left dome of the diaphragm in the left hypochondrium, related to the 9th through 11th ribs.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Pyramidal-shaped yellowish glandular tissue located retroperitoneally at the upper and medial pole of the right kidney, positioned directly behind the IVC.
questions.keyConcept: The right suprarenal (adrenal) gland is pyramidal in shape, capping the superior pole of the right kidney and lying immediately posterior to the IVC and right lobe of the liver.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Semilunar/crescentic yellowish endocrine gland situated on the medial border of the upper pole of the left kidney, lateral to the left crus of the diaphragm.
questions.keyConcept: The left suprarenal (adrenal) gland is semilunar in shape, extending along the medial border of the left kidney from the upper pole toward the hilum, related anteriorly to the stomach and pancreas.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Contrast radiographic examination (fluoroscopy/X-ray barium study) demonstrating opacification of the upper gastrointestinal tract including the stomach and duodenal cap via ingested barium contrast (barium meal).
questions.keyConcept: A barium meal is an upper gastrointestinal radiographic examination utilizing swallowed oral barium sulfate to evaluate the anatomy and mucosal contour of the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Plain radiograph / fluoroscopy showing complete retrograde filling and contrast opacification of the entire large intestine (rectum, sigmoid colon, descending colon, transverse colon, ascending colon, and caecum) via transrectal administration.
questions.keyConcept: A barium enema examination introduces radiopaque barium sulfate suspension through a rectal tube to outline the lumen, haustral mucosal pattern, and caliber of the entire large intestine.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 1 indicates the large blind-ended sac of the large intestine situated in the right iliac fossa below the ileocecal junction, continuous superiorly with the ascending colon.
questions.keyConcept: The caecum is the widest segment of the colon, lying intraperitoneally in the right iliac fossa; all three teniae coli converge at the base of the vermiform appendix on its posteromedial wall.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 3 indicates the vertical segment of the large intestine ascending through the right lumbar region along the right flank from the caecum to the right colic flexure.
questions.keyConcept: The ascending colon is secondarily retroperitoneal, covered anteriorly and on sides by peritoneum, and lies along the right paracolic gutter; it receives blood from the ileocolic and right colic arteries.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 4 indicates the right-angled junction situated in the right hypochondrium beneath the visceral surface of the liver, connecting the vertical ascending colon to the horizontal transverse colon.
questions.keyConcept: The right colic (hepatic) flexure lies lower and more anterior than the left colic flexure due to the overlying right lobe of the liver, and lies directly anterior to the lower pole of the right kidney.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 5 indicates the long, arched segment of the large intestine traversing the abdomen from the right hypochondrium across the umbilical region to the left hypochondrium.
questions.keyConcept: The transverse colon is completely intraperitoneal and mobile, suspended by the transverse mesocolon; its proximal two-thirds derive from the midgut (middle colic artery) and its distal third from the hindgut (left colic artery).

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 6 indicates the sharp bend situated high in the left hypochondrium at the junction of the transverse and descending colon, positioned beneath the spleen and resting on the phrenicocolic ligament.
questions.keyConcept: The left colic (splenic) flexure is attached to the diaphragm by the phrenicocolic ligament (sustentaculum lienis); it lies higher and deeper than the right flexure and marks the watershed zone between SMA and IMA territories (Griffiths' point).

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 7 indicates the vertical segment of the large intestine descending through the left lumbar region along the lateral border of the left kidney and psoas major down to the pelvic brim.
questions.keyConcept: The descending colon is secondarily retroperitoneal and fixed to the posterior abdominal wall, medially bordering the left paracolic gutter and supplied by the left colic artery of the IMA.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 8 indicates the S-shaped mobile loop of large intestine extending from the pelvic brim across the pelvic inlet to terminate at the level of the third sacral vertebra (S3).
questions.keyConcept: The sigmoid (pelvic) colon is freely mobile on its inverted V-shaped mesentery (sigmoid mesocolon); it is the most common site of colonic diverticula and volvulus.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 9 indicates the fixed terminal pelvic segment of the large intestine lying in the sacral concavity from the level of S3 down to the pelvic diaphragm.
questions.keyConcept: The rectum commences at vertebral level S3 as a continuation of the sigmoid colon; it lacks haustra, teniae coli, and epiploic appendages, possessing a complete outer longitudinal muscular coat.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 2 indicates the distal loop of small intestine ascending out of the pelvis to terminate into the posteromedial wall of the caecum at the ileocecal orifice.
questions.keyConcept: The terminal ileum enters the posteromedial aspect of the caecum at the ileocecal valve; it is characterized by prominent mucosal Peyer patches and is a common site for Crohn's disease and intussusception.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 1 indicates the dome-shaped superior portion of the stomach rising above the horizontal level of the cardiac notch, fitting under the left cupola of the diaphragm.
questions.keyConcept: The gastric fundus is the topmost curved part of the stomach above the cardiac orifice; on upright plain films, it contains swallowed air (the gastric air bubble or Magenblase) and is supplied by short gastric arteries from the splenic artery.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 2 indicates the large central vertical reservoir of the stomach bounded between the fundus above (horizontal plane through cardiac orifice) and the incisura angularis below.
questions.keyConcept: The body of the stomach makes up the largest anatomical region, lined by prominent rugae and containing gastric glands rich in parietal (acid-producing) and chief (pepsinogen-producing) cells.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 3 indicates the wide, slightly dilated proximal chamber of the pyloric part of the stomach extending from the angular incisure (incisura angularis) to the pyloric canal.
questions.keyConcept: The pyloric antrum forms the broad proximal division of the pyloric region that grinds and mixes food; it contains gastrin-secreting G-cells and funnels chyme toward the pyloric canal.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 4 indicates the narrow, constricted terminal muscular sphincter at the gastroduodenal junction marked by prominent circular muscle thickening at vertebral level L1.
questions.keyConcept: The pylorus is the distal anatomical sphincter of the stomach surrounded by a thickened ring of circular smooth muscle (pyloric sphincter) that controls gastric emptying into the duodenal bulb.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 5 indicates the triangular/conical smooth-walled first 2.5 cm of the duodenum immediately distal to the pyloric sphincter, filled with a smooth bolus of barium contrast.
questions.keyConcept: The duodenal cap (bulb) is the intraperitoneal, mobile first part of the duodenum; lacking plicae circulares, it presents a characteristic smooth triangular appearance on barium meal and is the primary site of peptic ulcer disease.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 6 indicates the vertical C-shaped segment of the duodenum descending from the superior duodenal flexure to the inferior duodenal flexure along the right side of vertebral bodies L1–L3.
questions.keyConcept: The second (descending) part of the duodenum is retroperitoneal and closely embraces the head of the pancreas; it receives the common bile duct and pancreatic duct at the major duodenal papilla.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 7 indicates coiled small bowel loops displaying a delicate, feathery mucosal flocculation of barium produced by closely packed, prominent circular folds (plicae circulares).
questions.keyConcept: The jejunum occupies primarily the umbilical and left upper abdominal quadrants, characterized radiologically by a feathery mucosal pattern due to tall, numerous plicae circulares (valvulae conniventes).

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Pointer 1 indicates the vertical segment of the large intestine ascending along the right side of the posterior abdominal wall with characteristic haustral sacculations.
questions.keyConcept: The ascending colon is secondarily retroperitoneal and extends from the caecum to the hepatic flexure, defined anatomically by sacculations (haustra) created by the teniae coli.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Pointer 2 indicates the broad, festooned loop of large intestine crossing the abdominal cavity horizontally between the right (hepatic) and left (splenic) colic flexures.
questions.keyConcept: The transverse colon is suspended by the transverse mesocolon, providing high mobility; its lumen exhibits characteristic transverse haustral folds on double-contrast barium radiography.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Pointer 3 indicates the vertical segment of the large intestine descending along the left flank from the splenic flexure to the pelvic brim.
questions.keyConcept: The descending colon lies retroperitoneally in the left lumbar gutter; it is narrower in caliber than the proximal colon and carries fecal contents into the sigmoid colon.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Fluoroscopic double-contrast barium enema radiograph demonstrating pointer 4 directed at the terminal, dilated midline pelvic reservoir of the large intestine (rectal ampulla / rectum), positioned in the true pelvis anterior to the sacrum and coccyx.
questions.keyConcept: The rectum begins at the rectosigmoid junction at the level of the S3 vertebra and terminates at the pelvic diaphragm / anorectal ring, lacking teniae coli, haustra, and appendices epiploicae.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Fluoroscopic double-contrast barium enema radiograph demonstrating pointer 5 directed at the redundant, mobile, S-shaped intraperitoneal loop of the large intestine (sigmoid colon) traversing the left iliac fossa and pelvic inlet toward the midline.
questions.keyConcept: The sigmoid colon is an intraperitoneal segment suspended by an inverted V-shaped mesocolon (sigmoid mesocolon) that conveys the sigmoid vessels and superior rectal artery.

questions.text: Identify the vertebral level of this abdominal CT cross-section:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Axial contrast-enhanced abdominal CT cross-section at the T12–L1 junction displaying the liver on the right, spleen and stomach on the left, portal vein bifurcation at the porta hepatis, and the abdominal aorta immediately anterior to the vertebral body giving off the celiac trunk.
questions.keyConcept: The celiac trunk arises from the anterior aspect of the abdominal aorta at the T12–L1 vertebral level immediately below the diaphragmatic aortic hiatus, giving off the left gastric, common hepatic, and splenic arteries.

questions.text: Identify the vertebral level of this abdominal CT cross-section:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Axial contrast-enhanced abdominal CT cross-section at the L1–L2 vertebral level (transpyloric plane) clearly displaying both kidneys with their renal hila and pelves, the horizontally traversing pancreatic body and tail, gallbladder fundus, and origin of the superior mesenteric artery.
questions.keyConcept: The transpyloric plane of Addison lies midway between the jugular notch and pubic symphysis (level of L1/L2 disc) and passes through the pylorus, pancreatic neck, origin of superior mesenteric artery, renal hila, and fundus of the gallbladder.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Clinical intraoral photographs of an infant demonstrating an intact upper lip with an abnormal midline fissure / cleft defect in the roof of the mouth involving the hard and soft palate.
questions.keyConcept: Cleft palate results from failure of the lateral palatine processes (palatal shelves) of the maxillary prominences to fuse with each other, the primary palate, and/or the nasal septum during the 7th to 10th weeks of gestation.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Clinical photograph of an infant demonstrating a unilateral vertical fissure / cleft of the upper lip on the left side extending toward the floor of the nostril.
questions.keyConcept: Unilateral cleft lip is the most common congenital craniofacial anomaly, caused by failure of the maxillary prominence on the affected side to fuse with the medial nasal prominence (intermaxillary segment) during the 5th to 6th weeks of embryonic development.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Clinical photograph of an infant demonstrating bilateral vertical clefts of the upper lip situated on both sides of an isolated central philtrum / prolabial segment.
questions.keyConcept: Bilateral cleft lip results from the bilateral failure of mesenchymal fusion between both maxillary prominences and the central medial nasal prominences (intermaxillary segment), leaving a protruding premaxillary prolabium.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Intraoral clinical photograph of a protruded tongue demonstrating a prominent midline cleft / notch dividing the anterior tip and body of the tongue into two symmetrical lobes.
questions.keyConcept: Bifid tongue (glossoschisis) is a congenital anomaly caused by incomplete or defective embryonic fusion of the two lateral lingual swellings (derived from the first pharyngeal arch) in the ventral midline during the 4th to 5th gestational weeks.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Clinical intraoral photograph of a newborn infant showing an abnormally short, thick lingual frenulum tethering the ventral tongue tip tightly to the floor of the mouth and mandibular alveolar ridge, restricting tongue elevation and protrusion.
questions.keyConcept: Ankyloglossia (tongue-tie) results from failure of normal apoptosis and degeneration of sublingual cells during development, leaving a short, tight lingual frenulum that impairs tongue mobility and infant breastfeeding latch.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Clinical photograph of a patient demonstrating generalized massive hypertrophy and enlargement of the tongue protruding markedly beyond the oral cavity and dental arches.
questions.keyConcept: Macroglossia is congenital or acquired tongue enlargement often associated with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, congenital hypothyroidism, or Down syndrome; caused by muscular hyperplasia, vascular malformations, or lymphangiomas.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Intraoral photograph of an open mouth demonstrating an abnormally small, rudimentary, hypoplastic tongue situated deep in the floor of the oral cavity.
questions.keyConcept: Microglossia (hypoglossia) is a rare congenital anomaly resulting from developmental arrest or hypoplasia of the embryonic lateral lingual swellings and tuberculum impar, frequently associated with micrognathia and limb anomalies.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Anatomical schematic diagram illustrating the classic morphological variants of tracheo-esophageal fistula (TEF) and esophageal atresia, most prominently showing a blind proximal esophageal pouch and a distal fistulous communication connecting the trachea to the lower esophagus.
questions.keyConcept: Tracheo-esophageal fistula (TEF) results from defective partitioning of the foregut by the tracheoesophageal septum during the 4th to 6th gestational weeks; the most common subtype (~85%) features proximal esophageal atresia with a distal fistula to the carina/trachea.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Coronal cross-sectional illustration of the distal thoracic esophagus demonstrating segmental luminal narrowing / stricture with sequential passage and balloon dilation using an esophageal dilator probe.
questions.keyConcept: Esophageal stenosis is congenital or acquired narrowing of the esophageal lumen, embryologically resulting from incomplete recanalization of the embryonic foregut lumen during the 8th week or vascular compromise; presents with progressive dysphagia.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Cut-away coronal schematic of the stomach and duodenum displaying massive hypertrophy of the circular smooth muscle layer of the pylorus severely narrowing the pyloric canal, with an indicator line marking the surgical pyloromyotomy (Ramstedt procedure) incision.
questions.keyConcept: Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (CHPS) presents classically in first-born males at 2–6 weeks of age with non-bilious projectile vomiting, an olive-shaped epigastric mass, and hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis due to marked hypertrophy of the circular pyloric muscularis.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Anatomical illustration demonstrating an abnormal stomach with a deep circumferential mid-gastric constriction dividing the organ into two distinct upper and lower pouches connected by a narrow central channel (hourglass stomach deformity).
questions.keyConcept: Hourglass stomach (bilocular stomach) is characterized by a central constriction dividing the stomach into proximal and distal compartments, typically resulting from cicatricial fibrosis and scarring secondary to chronic peptic ulcer disease along the lesser curvature.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Coronal illustration of the lower thorax and upper abdomen demonstrating herniation / cephalad protrusion of the gastroesophageal junction and gastric cardia through the diaphragmatic esophageal hiatus into the posterior mediastinum.
questions.keyConcept: Sliding hiatus hernia (type I) occurs when laxity or widening of the phrenoesophageal ligament allows the gastroesophageal junction and upper stomach to slide cephalad through the esophageal hiatus into the thoracic cavity, predisposing to gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Anatomical illustration demonstrating a ring-like collar of pancreatic parenchyma completely encircling the second (descending) part of the duodenum, causing extrinsic duodenal compression and proximal duodenal bulb dilation.
questions.keyConcept: Annular pancreas is a congenital anomaly caused by the failure of the ventral pancreatic bud to rotate properly with the duodenum during embryonic development (or persistence of a bifid ventral bud), forming a constricting ring around the second part of the duodenum that can cause duodenal obstruction.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Embryological schematic (diagram A) demonstrating persistence of the proximal (ileal) segment of the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct as a true blind-ending pouch arising from the anti-mesenteric border of the ileum, connected to the umbilicus by a fibrous band.
questions.keyConcept: Meckel's diverticulum is the most common congenital GI anomaly (rule of 2s: 2% prevalence, 2 inches long, 2 feet from ileocecal valve, can contain 2 types of ectopic mucosa: gastric and pancreatic) caused by failure of the proximal vitelline duct to obliterate.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Embryological schematic (diagram B) demonstrating fibrous cord obliteration of both the intestinal and umbilical ends of the vitelline duct, with persistence and cystic dilation of the patent intervening middle portion (vitelline cyst / enterocystoma).
questions.keyConcept: A vitelline cyst (omphalomesenteric duct cyst) develops when the intermediate segment of the vitelline duct remains patent while the umbilical and intestinal ends fibrously obliterate, forming a closed fluid-filled cyst suspended between the ileum and anterior abdominal wall.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Embryological schematic (diagram C) demonstrating complete failure of obliteration of the embryonic vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct along its entire length, producing a direct, continuous patent tubular communication between the ileal lumen and the umbilicus.
questions.keyConcept: A vitelline fistula (umbilical-ileal fistula) results from total non-closure of the embryonic vitelline duct, creating a direct conduit between the midgut lumen and the exterior that classically presents with neonatal fecal discharge from the umbilicus.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Full-thickness abdominal wall defect located immediately lateral (typically right) to the intact umbilical cord insertion, through which bowel loops herniate freely without a covering peritoneal or amniotic sac.
questions.keyConcept: Gastroschisis is a congenital abdominal wall defect caused by failure of lateral abdominal fold fusion or vascular disruption, leaving herniated viscera exposed directly to amniotic fluid without an enclosing membrane.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Midline anterior abdominal wall defect at the base of the umbilical ring, where herniated abdominal contents are enclosed within a translucent membranous sac of peritoneum and amnion with the umbilical cord inserting at its apex.
questions.keyConcept: Omphalocele occurs when midgut loops fail to return from the physiological umbilical hernia during the 10th-11th gestational week; unlike gastroschisis, it is midline, covered by a peritoneal-amniotic sac, and strongly associated with karyotypic and cardiac anomalies.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Absence of a patent anal orifice at the anatomical perineal verge, with smooth or dimpled skin overlying the expected anal region.
questions.keyConcept: Imperforate anus (anorectal malformation) results from failure of the anal membrane to perforate or abnormal development/partitioning of the embryonic cloaca and urorectal septum.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Sagittal section of the male pelvis demonstrating a persistent fistulous communication connecting the blind-ending terminal rectum to the posterior aspect of the prostatic urethra, with an imperforate perineal anus.
questions.keyConcept: Rectourethral fistula is the most common anorectal malformation in males, occurring due to incomplete caudal division of the cloaca by the urorectal septum, leading to meconium-stained urine.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Sagittal section of the female pelvis demonstrating a fistulous communication between the anterior wall of the terminal rectum and the posterior wall of the vagina, accompanied by an imperforate anus.
questions.keyConcept: Rectovaginal fistula develops when the urorectal septum fails to completely partition the cloaca between the rectum and the developing uterovaginal canal, allowing meconium and feces to pass through the vaginal introitus.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Sagittal pelvic section demonstrating a high anorectal defect where a persistent fistulous tract connects the rectum directly into the base/posterior wall of the urinary bladder (above the prostate), with an imperforate perineal anus.
questions.keyConcept: Rectovesical fistula is a high-type anorectal malformation resulting from early arrest of the urorectal septum's descent, creating direct communication between the hindgut and the urinary bladder cavity.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Diagram of the biliary apparatus demonstrating a duplicated/bifurcated gallbladder containing two distinct gallbladder bodies/lumens arising from the cystic duct.
questions.keyConcept: Double gallbladder (vesica fellea duplex) is a congenital anatomical variant caused by premature bifurcated branching or supernumerary budding of the cystic diverticulum from the common bile duct.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Biliary tract diagram showing severe narrowing and fibrous cord obliteration of the common bile duct terminating toward the second part of the duodenum.
questions.keyConcept: Obliteration of the bile duct (extrahepatic biliary atresia) results from failure of the embryonic biliary cords to recanalize or progressive perinatal inflammatory fibrosis, causing persistent neonatal cholestasis, acholic stools, and dark urine.

questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Gastroduodenal diagram showing complete luminal occlusion (atresia) of the duodenum with marked compensatory dilation of the proximal duodenal bulb and stomach.
questions.keyConcept: Duodenal atresia arises from failure of the solid-stage duodenal lumen to recanalize during the 8th to 10th weeks of gestation; classically produces neonatal bilious vomiting and the radiologic 'double-bubble' sign, and is strongly associated with Down syndrome (Trisomy 21).
